title: Dots and vowels
hook: dots and vowel marks were added later to help new readers

segments.voice: Yesterday, mushaf: Uthman's copies, one standard sent out to the cities. Your line was one text, many cities. Day three hundred eighteen.

Three Arabic letters: ba, ta, tha. In a modern mushaf they have exactly the same shape, a little boat. The only difference is the dots: one below for ba, two above for ta, three above for tha. Now take the dots away. That's close to what the earliest copies looked like: the bones of the words, with the reader supplying the rest from what they'd learned by ear.
screen: `BA, TA, THA: ONE SHAPE.` → `ONLY THE DOTS DIFFER.` → `NOW TAKE THE DOTS AWAY.`

segments.voice: Early Arabic writing was a kind of shorthand. Many letters shared a shape, the dots that tell them apart were used sparingly, and short vowels weren't written at all. For the first Muslims that wasn't a problem: the Qur'an lived in their mouths, learned from teachers, and the page was a reminder of what they already knew. But as Islam spread to people whose first language wasn't Arabic, the tradition says, mistakes in recitation began. Tradition credits a scholar of Basra, Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali, in the first Islamic century, with the first vowel marks: colored dots, often red, placed above, below or beside a letter to show its sound. Later, in the time of the governor al-Hajjaj, scholars are said to have added the dots that tell similar letters apart more fully. In the next century, al-Khalil ibn Ahmad of Basra, who also mapped the meters of Arabic poetry, gave the vowels the small shapes still used today: a slanting stroke above, a tiny curl like a waw, a stroke below. Sources tell the details differently. But in every telling, the text itself stays put: the marks were added around it, like pronunciation guides on a poem for a new reader. Some scholars at the time disliked writing anything extra inside the mushaf. In the end the community accepted the marks, because they served the recitation that had been passed down. Each dot was put there for a learner.
screen: `THE SAME SHAPE, DIFFERENT DOTS` · `A PAGE THAT REMINDED, NOT TAUGHT` · `RED DOTS FOR VOWELS` · `MARKS ADDED AROUND THE TEXT`

segments.voice: If you have a mushaf or an app, open any page and just look, without trying to read: find the dots, one, two, three, above and below, and the tiny vowel strokes. If there's no page in front of you, bring to mind ba, ta and tha, three little boats told apart only by their dots.
Tashkil. Vowel marking — the small strokes added to the Qur'an's script so new readers could recite it rightly. Today's word.
Your line: marks for the reader. The words stayed; the help was added around them. Day three hundred eighteen, done.

howItsDone: Muslims today read from copies with full dots and vowel marks, and learners, especially those who didn't grow up with Arabic, rely on those marks to recite correctly.

fork.setup: you teach the Qur'an in Basra. new Muslims who didn't grow up with Arabic keep misreading the vowels. what do you do?
options: change the words to easier ones.
add small marks to show the sounds.
fork.reveal: tradition says that's exactly what Abu al-Aswad did: colored dots for the vowels, with the words untouched.

original.note: Arabic: vowel marking, the small strokes that show short vowels. the dots that tell letters apart are called i'jam.

trapdoor: what you thought: Arabic script always looked like this.
what it means: dots and vowel marks added over the first centuries to help new readers recite correctly.
what a scholar hears: i'jam and tashkil, credited in tradition to Abu al-Aswad, the circle of al-Hajjaj and al-Khalil, though the sources differ on who did what, and when.
recall: one of the Qur'an's 114 named chapters
recitation: the thing that is read aloud

chat.says: Why do the letters in a Qur'an have little dots and strokes?
options: They were added later around the text, so new readers could recite it rightly.
They're decorations by the scribes, and they don't change how a word is read.
They were in the very first copies, written out by the Prophet ﷺ himself.
chat.meaning: Early writing left out short vowels and many dots. Marks were added around the text so learners could recite it as it was passed down.

tashkil.meaning: vowel marking: the small strokes that show short vowels

Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali.meaning: a scholar of Basra credited with the first vowel marks

al-Khalil ibn Ahmad.meaning: a scholar of Basra who gave vowels their shapes used today

al-Hajjaj.meaning: a governor in whose time more letter dots were added

Basra.meaning: a city in Iraq where early scholars of Arabic worked

notes: Attributions (Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali, d. c. 69 AH; Nasr ibn Asim and Yahya ibn Ya'mur under al-Hajjaj; al-Khalil ibn Ahmad, d. c. 170 AH) follow the traditional account; sources vary. Confirm.
Early manuscripts with sparse consonant dots: a general statement; confirm.
The description of the modern vowel shapes (fatha, damma, kasra) is simplified for listeners.
